a: Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy that investigates the fundamental nature of reality, existence, and the world. It addresses the most basic questions about what exists and what it means for something to exist. Ontology is the study of being and existence, examining categories of being, the nature of objects and their properties, and whether abstract entities like numbers, universals, and possibilities exist. Cosmology, in the philosophical sense, investigates the origin, structure, and ultimate fate of the universe as a whole, asking questions about why there is something rather than nothing and whether the universe has a purpose. Aristotle called metaphysics the first philosophy because it deals with the most fundamental principles underlying all other knowledge.

The free will versus determinism debate asks whether human actions are freely chosen or determined by prior causes. Determinism holds that every event, including human decisions, is causally necessitated by preceding events and natural laws. Hard determinism concludes that free will is an illusion because determinism is true. Libertarian free will argues that humans have genuine free choice and determinism is false. Compatibilism attempts to reconcile the two by redefining free will as acting according to one's own desires without external coercion. The mind-body problem concerns the relationship between mental phenomena and physical bodies. Dualism, associated with Descartes, holds that mind and matter are distinct substances that interact. Physicalism (materialism) argues that mental states are entirely produced by brain activity and there is no non-physical mind.

q: what makes you the same person
a: Personal identity examines what makes a person the same individual over time despite constant physical and psychological change. The psychological continuity theory, favored by John Locke, holds that continuity of memory, personality, and consciousness defines personal identity. The bodily continuity theory argues that physical continuity of the body or brain is what matters. The ship of Theseus thought experiment challenges these views: if all parts of a ship are replaced over time, is it still the same ship? The philosophy of time explores whether time is real and what its nature is. Presentism holds that only the present moment exists. Eternalism (the block universe theory) holds that past, present, and future all exist equally. The A-theory of time treats the present as objectively special, while the B-theory treats all moments as equally real.

Causality is the relationship between cause and effect, a central topic in metaphysics. David Hume argued that we never directly observe causation but only perceive constant conjunction of events, leading to the problem of induction and skepticism about causal necessity. Possible worlds semantics, developed by David Lewis and others, treats possible worlds as concrete or abstract entities that represent alternative ways the world could have been. Leibniz famously argued that this is the best of all possible worlds. Abstract objects are non-physical, non-mental entities that exist outside space and time, such as numbers, mathematical truths, propositions, and Platonic Forms. The debate about whether abstract objects exist independently of human thought (Platonic realism) or are human constructions (nominalism) remains a fundamental issue in metaphysics.
